Sulfur: extract + sodium nitroprusside → violet color.
Halogens: extract + HNO₃ + AgNO₃ → precipitate (AgCl white, AgBr pale yellow, AgI yellow).
mustKnow: Nitrogen test: Prussian blue confirms N.
Sulfur test: violet coloration confirms S.
Halogen test: silver halide precipitate confirms halogen; color identifies which halogen.
examTraps: Do not confuse the Prussian blue test — it is specific to nitrogen, not any metal ion.
If both nitrogen and sulfur are present, the blood-red color from FeSCN²⁺ may appear instead of Prussian blue.

summary: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. This block covers alkanes (saturated, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂), alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ), alkynes (CₙH₂ₙ₋₂), petroleum chemistry, and structural/geometric isomerism.

subtopics.title: Alkanes (Paraffins)
keyPoints: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
C₁–C₄: gases; C₅–C₁₇: liquids; C₁₈ₚ: solids at room temperature.
Boiling point increases with chain length due to increased Van der Waals forces.
Branched alkanes have lower boiling points than straight-chain isomers.
Alkanes are relatively unreactive (hence 'paraffins' = little affinity).
Combustion: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + (3n+1)/2 O₂ → n CO₂ + (n+1) H₂O + heat.
Substitution (halogenation): RH + X₂ → RX + HX (e.g., CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl).
Cracking: large alkanes break into smaller alkanes and alkenes (e.g., C₁₆H₃₄ → C₈H₁₈ + C₈H₁₆).
mustKnow: IUPAC naming: find the longest continuous carbon chain (parent name).
Number the chain to give substituents the lowest possible numbers.
Use prefixes (di-, tri-, tetra-) for multiple identical substituents.
Common substituents: methyl (CH₃—), ethyl (C₂H₅—), propyl (C₃H₇—).
examTraps: Do not forget to use commas between numbers and hyphens between numbers and letters (e.g., 2,3-dimethylpentane).
Do not include the carbon of the functional group when naming the parent chain for alkanes — all carbons are in the chain.

subtopics.title: Petroleum Chemistry
keyPoints: Petroleum (crude oil) is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons formed from ancient marine organisms.
Fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions based on boiling point differences.
Fractions (from lowest to highest boiling point): refinery gases (C₁–C₄), gasoline (C₅–C₁₀), kerosene (C₁₁–C₁₃), diesel (C₁₄–C₁₈), fuel oil (C₁₉–C₂₅), bitumen (C₂₆ₚ).
Cracking breaks large hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful ones (e.g., gasoline).
Catalytic cracking uses zeolite catalysts for better efficiency than thermal cracking.
Reforming converts straight-chain alkanes into branched alkanes or aromatics (improves octane rating).
Octane rating measures a fuel's resistance to knocking; higher = better.
mustKnow: LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) = propane + butane.
Gasoline (petrol) = C₅–C₁₀ hydrocarbons.
Kerosene (paraffin oil) = C₁₁–C₁₃, used as jet fuel.
Diesel = C₁₄–C₁₈, used in diesel engines.
examTraps: Do not confuse cracking (breaking large molecules) with reforming (restructuring molecules).
Fractional distillation is a PHYSICAL separation, not a chemical reaction.

subtopics.title: Alkenes (Olefins)
keyPoints: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with at least one C=C double bond (general formula CₙH₂ₙ).
Functional group: C=C (one sigma + one pi bond).
Naming: use -ene suffix; indicate double-bond position with a number (e.g., but-1-ene).
Geometric (cis-trans) isomerism: different arrangement of groups across the double bond.
cis isomer: similar groups on the same side of the double bond.
trans isomer: similar groups on opposite sides of the double bond.
Addition reactions (electrophilic addition): H₂ (hydrogenation), X₂ (halogenation), HX (hydrohalogenation), H₂O (hydration).
Hydrogenation: alkene + H₂ → alkane (used to convert unsaturated fats to saturated).
Markovnikov's rule: in HX addition to an unsymmetrical alkene, the H attaches to the carbon with more H atoms already.
mustKnow: Ethene (C₂H₄) is the simplest alkene — used to make polyethylene (addition polymerisation).
Test for unsaturation: bromine water (Br₂) decolorises from red-brown to colourless with alkenes.
Baeyer's test: cold dilute KMnO₄ changes from purple to colourless with alkenes (dihydroxylation).
examTraps: Alkenes do NOT undergo substitution reactions easily — they undergo ADDITION.
Do NOT say alkene + Br₂ gives a substitution product — it gives a dibromoalkane (addition).
Alkanes undergo substitution (halogenation); alkenes undergo addition.

subtopics.title: Alkynes
keyPoints: Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with at least one C≡C triple bond (general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂).
Functional group: C≡C (one sigma + two pi bonds).
Naming: use -yne suffix (e.g., ethyne, propyne).
Addition reactions: can add 1 or 2 moles of H₂, X₂, HX.
Ethyne (acetylene, C₂H₂) is the simplest alkyne — used in welding (oxy-acetylene flame).
Terminal alkynes (C≡C—H) are acidic (weak) and can form metal acetylides (e.g., with Ag⁺, Cu⁺).
mustKnow: Ethyne + H₂ (Lindlar's catalyst) → ethene (cis-alkene).
Ethyne + 2H₂ → ethane.
Terminal alkynes give white (Ag₂C₂) or red (Cu₂C₂) precipitates with ammoniacal AgNO₃ or Cu₂Cl₂.
examTraps: Do not confuse ethyne (C₂H₂) with ethene (C₂H₄) — ethyne has a triple bond, ethene has a double bond.
Alkynes are MORE unsaturated than alkenes — they add two moles of halogen, not one.

subtopics.title: Isomerism
keyPoints: Structural isomerism: same molecular formula, different connectivity of atoms.
Types: chain (carbon skeleton varies), position (functional group position varies), functional group (different functional groups).
Geometric (cis-trans) isomerism: same connectivity but different spatial arrangement due to restricted rotation around a double bond.
Conditions for geometric isomerism: each carbon of the double bond must have two different groups attached.
mustKnow: Example of chain isomerism: C₅H₁₂ (n-pentane, isopentane, neopentane).
Example of position isomerism: C₃H₇OH (propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol).
Example of functional group isomerism: C₂H₆O (ethanol and methoxymethane/dimethyl ether).
examTraps: Do not confuse structural and geometric isomerism — geometric requires a double bond with restricted rotation.
cis-trans isomers are NOT the same as conformational isomers (which rotate freely).

summary: This block covers alkanols (alcohols, —OH), phenols (—OH attached to benzene), and alkoxyalkanes (ethers, —O—). Topics include classification, hydrogen bonding, reactivity, and key reactions.

subtopics.title: Alkanols (Alcohols)
keyPoints: Alkanols contain the hydroxyl (—OH) functional group attached to an sp³ carbon.
General formula: R—OH (R = alkyl group).
Classification: primary (1°), secondary (2°), tertiary (3°) based on how many carbons the —OH carbon is bonded to.
Hydrogen bonding between —OH groups gives alcohols higher boiling points than alkanes.
Solubility: lower alcohols (C₁–C₃) are water-miscible; solubility decreases as chain length increases.
Combustion: alcohols burn to give CO₂ + H₂O.
Oxidation: primary alcohols → aldehydes → carboxylic acids; secondary → ketones; tertiary do not oxidise easily.
Dehydration: alcohol + conc. H₂SO₄ → alkene + H₂O (elimination, follows Zaitsev's rule).
Esterification: alcohol + carboxylic acid → ester + H₂O (with conc. H₂SO₄).
mustKnow: Oxidising agent: K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺ (orange → green colour change confirms oxidation).
Primary alcohol → aldehyde (distillation) → carboxylic acid (reflux).
Secondary alcohol → ketone (cannot be oxidised further without breaking C—C bonds).
Tertiary alcohol → resistant to oxidation.
Iodoform test: ethanol and secondary alcohols with CH₃CHOH— give yellow precipitate of CHI₃.
examTraps: Do not say alcohols are acidic — they are very weakly acidic (pKa~16), weaker than water.
Dehydration of a primary alcohol gives the least substituted alkene (anti-Zaitsev), but secondary/tertiary follow Zaitsev's rule (most substituted alkene).
Do not confuse hydration (alkene + H₂O → alcohol) with dehydration (alcohol → alkene + H₂O).

subtopics.title: Phenols
keyPoints: Phenol: —OH group directly attached to a benzene ring (C₆H₅OH).
Phenol is a stronger acid than alcohols (pKa~10 vs alcohol pKa~16) due to resonance stabilisation of phenoxide ion.

Reactions: (a) weak acid — dissolves in NaOH but not NaHCO₃. (b) Bromination — with Br₂ water gives white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol. (c) Nitration — gives a mixture of ortho- and para-nitrophenol. (d) Coupling — with diazonium salts gives azo dyes (orange/red colour).
Ferric chloride test: phenol + FeCl₃ → violet/purple colouration (characteristic test).
mustKnow: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol but weaker than carboxylic acids.
2,4,6-tribromophenol is a white precipitate — a confirmatory test for phenol.
examTraps: Do not classify phenol as a typical alcohol — its chemistry is distinct due to the aromatic ring.
Phenol does NOT undergo esterification as readily as alcohols.

subtopics.title: Alkoxyalkanes (Ethers)
keyPoints: Ethers have the general formula R—O—R' where R and R' are alkyl or aryl groups.
Naming: alkoxyalkane (e.g., methoxyethane) or common names (e.g., diethyl ether, methyl phenyl ether).
Ethers are relatively unreactive (used as solvents).
They can form peroxides on exposure to air (danger of explosion on distillation).
Cleavage: ethers react with conc. HI or HBr to give alkyl halides and alcohols.
Ethers do NOT form hydrogen bonds with each other (no O—H) but can accept hydrogen bonds from water (limited solubility).
Boiling points are lower than alcohols of similar mass (no intermolecular hydrogen bonding).
mustKnow: Diethyl ether (C₂H₅OC₂H₅) was used as an anaesthetic.
Ethers are polar but aprotic — useful as solvents for Grignard reactions.

topic: Block 4: Carbonyl Compounds and Carboxylic Acids
summary: This block covers aldehydes (RCHO), ketones (RCOR'), carboxylic acids (RCOOH), and their derivatives (esters, acyl halides, amides). Focus on nucleophilic addition, oxidation/reduction, and acidity trends.

subtopics.title: Aldehydes and Ketones
keyPoints: Both contain the carbonyl group (C=O). Aldehydes have at least one H on the carbonyl carbon; ketones have two alkyl/aryl groups.
Naming: aldehydes use -al suffix (e.g., methanal, ethanal); ketones use -one (e.g., propanone).
Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones due to less steric hindrance and greater polarisation.
Nucleophilic addition: carbonyl + HCN → cyanohydrin; + NaHSO₃ → bisulfite adduct; + NH₂OH → oxime.
Reduction: aldehyde/ketone + NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ → alcohol.
Oxidation: aldehydes oxidise easily to carboxylic acids; ketones resist oxidation.
Tollens' test: aldehyde + ammoniacal AgNO₃ → silver mirror (Ag deposited).
Fehling's test: aldehyde + Cu²⁺ (blue) → Cu₂O (red precipitate); ketones do NOT react.
Iodoform test: methyl ketones (CH₃COR) + I₂/NaOH → yellow precipitate of CHI₃.
mustKnow: Methanal (HCHO) is a gas; ethanal (CH₃CHO) and propanone are liquids.
Propanone ((CH₃)₂CO) is the simplest ketone — used as a solvent (nail polish remover).
Tollens' reagent = ammoniacal silver nitrate; Fehling's reagent = Cu²⁺ in alkaline tartrate.
examTraps: Do not say ketones reduce Tollens' reagent — only aldehydes do.
Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones in nucleophilic addition — explain why (steric + electronic).

subtopics.title: Carboxylic Acids
keyPoints: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group (—COOH) and have general formula RCOOH or CₙH₂ₙO₂.
Naming: alkanoic acids (e.g., methanoic acid HCOOH, ethanoic acid CH₃COOH).
Acidity: carboxylic acids are stronger than phenols and alcohols due to resonance stabilisation of the carboxylate anion.
Acidity decreases as alkyl chain length increases (electron-donating effect).
Electron-withdrawing groups (—Cl, —F, —NO₂) increase acidity by stabilising the conjugate base.
Reactions: neutralisation (acid + base → salt + water), esterification (alcohol + acid → ester), reduction (LiAlH₄ → alcohol), decarboxylation (heat → CO₂).
mustKnow: Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) is the main component of vinegar.
Methanoic acid (HCOOH) is present in ant venom and nettle stings.
Ka measures acid strength; larger Ka = stronger acid.
pKa = −log Ka; smaller pKa = stronger acid.
examTraps: Do not confuse the reactivity of —COOH in carboxylic acids with —OH in alcohols — the —OH in —COOH is more acidic due to the adjacent C=O.
Carboxylic acids do NOT undergo nucleophilic addition like aldehydes/ketones — the carbonyl in RCOOH is less electrophilic due to resonance with the —OH group.

subtopics.title: Esters
keyPoints: Esters have the general formula RCOOR' and are formed by condensation of a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.
Naming: alkyl alkanoate (e.g., ethyl ethanoate CH₃COOC₂H₅).
Fruity smell: esters are responsible for many fruit flavours and fragrances.
Hydrolysis: ester + H₂O (acid or base) → acid + alcohol. Base hydrolysis (saponification) is irreversible.
Transesterification: ester + alcohol → new ester + new alcohol.
mustKnow: Saponification: ester + NaOH → sodium salt of carboxylic acid + alcohol (soap-making).
Biodiesel is produced by transesterification of vegetable oils.

topic: Block 5: Alkanamines and Advanced Carbon Structures
summary: This block covers alkanamines (amines, —NH₂), their basicity and reactions, as well as advanced carbon allotropes such as fullerenes and the pharmaceutical relevance of organic compounds.

subtopics.title: Alkanamines (Amines)
keyPoints: Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia (NH₃) where alkyl or aryl groups replace one or more hydrogens.
Classification: primary (1°, RNH₂), secondary (2°, R₂NH), tertiary (3°, R₃N).
Naming: alkanamines (e.g., methanamine CH₃NH₂, ethanamine C₂H₅NH₂).
Amines are basic due to the lone pair on nitrogen — they accept protons (H⁺).
Basicity: aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia; aromatic amines (e.g., aniline) are weaker due to resonance delocalisation of the lone pair.
Alkylation: amine + alkyl halide → more highly substituted amine (can go to quaternary ammonium salt R₄N⁺X⁻).
Acylation: amine + acyl chloride → amide (e.g., CH₃COCl + CH₃NH₂ → CH₃CONHCH₃ + HCl).
Carbylamine reaction: primary amine + CHCl₃ + KOH → isocyanide (foul-smelling).
Carbylamine test distinguishes 1° amines from 2° and 3° amines.
mustKnow: Quaternary ammonium salts (R₄N⁺X⁻) are used as phase-transfer catalysts and surfactants.
Aniline (C₆H₅NH₂) is the simplest aromatic amine — weaker base than aliphatic amines.
Amine salts (formed with HCl) are water-soluble and crystalline.
examTraps: Do not say all amines are stronger bases than ammonia — aromatic amines are WEAKER.
Carbylamine test is ONLY positive for 1° amines — 2° and 3° do NOT give isocyanides.
Acylation of 1° or 2° amines gives amides, but tertiary amines cannot form amides (no H on N).

subtopics.title: Fullerenes and Advanced Carbon
keyPoints: Fullerenes are allotropes of carbon with cage-like structures (C₆₀, C₇₀).
C₆₀ (buckminsterfullerene) is a spherical molecule with 60 carbon atoms arranged in pentagons and hexagons (like a football).
Fullerenes are used in materials science, electronics, and medicine (drug delivery).
Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are cylindrical fullerenes with exceptional strength and conductivity.
mustKnow: Fullerenes are different from diamond and graphite — they are the third crystalline form of carbon.
C₆₀ is also called 'buckyball' after Buckminster Fuller.
examTraps: Do not confuse allotropes of carbon: diamond (sp³), graphite (sp² layers), fullerenes (sp² cages).

topic: Block 6: Atomic Foundations and Quantum Mechanics
summary: This block covers the fundamental structure of the atom and the mathematical rules governing electron placement: subatomic particles, orbital shapes and capacities, quantum numbers, and electronic configuration rules.

subtopics.title: Subatomic Particles and Orbitals
keyPoints: Protons: positively charged, located in the nucleus.
Neutrons: neutrally charged, located in the nucleus.
Electrons: negatively charged, occupying orbitals around the nucleus.
s-orbital: spherical, holds 2 electrons, 1 orbital per subshell.
p-orbital: dumbbell-shaped, holds 6 electrons, 3 orbitals per subshell.
d-orbital: holds 10 electrons, 5 orbitals per subshell.
f-orbital: holds 14 electrons, 7 orbitals per subshell.
mustKnow: Maximum electrons per shell = 2n².
Each orbital holds a maximum of 2 electrons (Pauli's principle).
The d-sublevel has 5 orbitals; the f-sublevel has 7 orbitals.

subtopics.title: Quantum Numbers
keyPoints: Principal quantum number (n): energy level/shell size (n = 1, 2, 3, ...).
Azimuthal quantum number (l): subshell shape (l = 0 → s, 1 → p, 2 → d, 3 → f).
Magnetic quantum number (mₗ): orbital orientation (-l to +l, including 0).
Spin quantum number (mₛ): electron spin (+½ or -½).
Aufbau Principle: electrons fill orbitals from lowest to highest energy.
Hund's Rule: degenerate orbitals are filled singly before pairing electrons.
Pauli Exclusion Principle: no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers.
mustKnow: For n=1, only l=0 (1s) is possible — there is no 1p orbital.
For n=3: possible l values are 0 (3s), 1 (3p), 2 (3d).
In many-electron atoms, orbitals on the same energy level are NOT degenerate due to electron-electron repulsion.

subtopics.title: Electronic Configuration
keyPoints: Filling order: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p.
Notation: 1s² means 2 electrons in the 1s subshell (n=1, l=0).
Valence electrons: electrons in the outermost shell (determines chemical properties).
A full valence shell contains 8 electrons (s²p⁶) except for H and He (duplet rule, 2 electrons).
Anomalous configurations: Cr ([Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵) and Cu ([Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰).
mustKnow: Sodium (Z=11): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ or [Ne]3s¹.
Iron (Z=26): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶ or [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶.
Potassium (Z=19): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹ — 4s fills before 3d.
Co²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁷ (electrons removed from 4s first).
For ions, electrons are removed from the 4s orbital BEFORE the 3d orbital.

topic: Block 7: The Periodic Table and Periodicity
summary: This block focuses on the organization of elements and predictable trends in their physical and chemical properties: historical development, classification of elements, and periodic trends.

subtopics.title: Historical Development
keyPoints: Johann Dobereiner (1829): grouped elements into triads (e.g., Li, Na, K) based on similar properties.
John Newlands (1864): Law of Octaves — compared elements to musical notes.
Dmitri Mendeleev: arranged elements by increasing atomic mass, left gaps for undiscovered elements, predicted their properties.
Henry Moseley (1913): arranged modern table by increasing atomic number using X-ray frequencies.
mustKnow: Mendeleev's table was organized by chemical behavior, not just atomic mass.
Moseley's work corrected inconsistencies in Mendeleev's table.
Modern table: arranged by increasing atomic number.

subtopics.title: Classification of Elements
keyPoints: Main group (representative) elements: Groups 1A–7A (old) or 1, 2, 13–18 (IUPAC).
Transition elements: Groups 1B–8B (d-block), e.g., Titanium, Iron, Copper.
Inner transition elements: Lanthanides and Actinides (f-block).
Metals on left/centre; non-metals on right; metalloids along staircase (Boron, Silicon).
Periods: horizontal rows. Groups/families: vertical columns.
mustKnow: Group 1A (Alkali Metals): Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr — 1 valence electron.
Group 2A (Alkaline Earth Metals): Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra — 2 valence electrons.
Group 7A (Halogens): F, Cl, Br, I, At — diatomic, form salts.
Group 8A (Noble Gases): He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn — monatomic, filled valence shells.
examTraps: Hydrogen and Helium follow the duplet rule (2 electrons), not the octet rule.
Bromine is the only liquid halogen at room temperature.
Bismuth (Group 5A) is a metal — not all Group 5A elements are non-metals.

subtopics.title: Periodic Trends
keyPoints: Atomic radius: decreases across a period (higher Z_eff); increases down a group (more shells).
Ionization energy: increases across a period; decreases down a group.
Electron affinity: Chlorine has the highest EA (not Fluorine, due to size/repulsion).
Ionic radius: cations < parent atoms; anions > parent atoms.
For isoelectronic species: N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ (radius decreases as nuclear charge increases).
mustKnow: In period 3: Argon has highest ionization energy (full octet); Sodium has lowest.
Sulfur has LOWER ionization energy than Phosphorus (electron from doubly occupied p-orbital).
Oxygen has LOWER ionization energy than Nitrogen (same reason).
examTraps: Fluorine has a LOWER electron affinity than Chlorine.
Ionization energy exceptions occur at Group 2 (filled s) and Group 5 (half-filled p).

summary: A detailed look at specific families of elements and their unique behaviors: alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, halogens, noble gases, and groups 3A-6A.

subtopics.title: Group 1A — Alkali Metals
keyPoints: Highly reactive, low melting points, +1 oxidation state.
Never found pure in nature due to low ionization energy and high reactivity.
Reactivity INCREASES down the group (larger atomic radius, easier to lose valence electron).
React with oxygen to form metal oxides (Li₂O), peroxides (Na₂O₂), or superoxides (KO₂).
React vigorously with water to form alkaline solutions and H₂ gas: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.
Lithium is unique: forms stable nitride (Li₃N).
mustKnow: All form +1 ions.
Group 1A metals displace all metals below them in the reactivity series.

subtopics.title: Group 2A — Alkaline Earth Metals
keyPoints: Less reactive than Group 1A; +2 oxidation state.
Beryllium and Magnesium belong here; Magnesium is found in chlorophyll.
Reactivity increases down the group as valence electrons are held more loosely.
Calcium used to remove nitrogen from argon and as a reducing agent.
Mg is used in car engines; Ca is used in production of cement and bleaching powder.
mustKnow: They are less reactive than Group 1A because it requires more energy to remove two electrons.
MgO + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂O (neutralization of basic oxide).

subtopics.title: Groups 3A-8A
keyPoints: Group 3A: Boron is a metalloid; Aluminum forms Al³⁺ in acid.
Group 4A (C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb): Carbon shows considerable variation from non-metallic to metallic. Sn and Pb react with acids to produce H₂. Oxidation states +2 and +4.
Group 5A: Nitrogen and Phosphorus form HNO₃ and H₃PO₄. Bismuth is a metal.
Group 6A (Oxygen family): Oxygen is gas; Tellurium and Polonium are crystalline.
Group 7A (Halogens): All diatomic, form ionic salts; F₂ is most reactive, I₂ least. Reactivity with hydrogen decreases down the group.
Halogen displacement: Cl₂ displaces Br₂ and I₂; Br₂ displaces I₂ (halogen acts as oxidizing agent).
Group 8A (Noble Gases): Monatomic, filled valence shells. Xenon compounds first formed in 1963.
mustKnow: Noble gases are chemically stable due to filled valence shells.
Halogens form ionic salts with metals (metal is reducing agent).
Bromine is the only liquid halogen.

summary: Focuses on the d-block elements and their complex chemical properties: variable oxidation states, colored compounds, catalytic activity, crystal field theory, and complex ions.

subtopics.title: General Characteristics
keyPoints: Transition elements are d-block elements (Groups 1B, 3B-8B).
They serve as a bridge between Groups II and III in the periodic table.
General characteristics: variable oxidation states, formation of colored complexes, paramagnetism.
Examples: Titanium, Iron, Copper, Scandium.
Scandium configuration: [Ar] 4s² 3d¹.
mustKnow: Iron has BCC crystal structure at room temperature.
Transition metals often act as catalysts in industrial processes.
Colored compounds arise from d-d electron transitions.

subtopics.title: Crystal Field Theory and Magnetism
keyPoints: In octahedral fields, d-orbitals split into t₂g and e_g sets.
Unpaired electrons lead to paramagnetic behavior.
Magnetic moment calculated using spin-only formula: μ_s = √(n(n+2)) BM, where n = number of unpaired electrons.
The number of unpaired electrons determines the magnetic properties.
mustKnow: Paramagnetic: attracted to magnetic fields (has unpaired electrons).
Diamagnetic: not attracted (all electrons paired).
Higher number of unpaired electrons = stronger magnetic moment.

subtopics.title: Complex Ions
keyPoints: Complex ions: central metal ion surrounded by ligands.
Ligands: Lewis bases that donate electron pairs to the metal.
Coordination number: number of ligand donor atoms bonded to the metal.
Common geometries: octahedral (coordination number 6), tetrahedral (coordination number 4).
mustKnow: Ligands bond to metals via coordinate covalent bonds.
The charge of a complex ion = sum of metal ion charge + ligand charges.

topic: Block 10: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Geometry
summary: This block explores how atoms combine and the resulting shapes of molecules: Lewis structures, VSEPR theory, hybridization, and the octet rule.

subtopics.title: Lewis Structures and the Octet Rule
keyPoints: Lewis structures use dot notation to represent valence electrons.
Atoms bond to achieve a full valence shell (octet rule: 8 electrons).
Exceptions: H and He follow duplet rule (2 electrons).
Covalent bonds: sharing of electron pairs between atoms.
Ionic bonds: transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal.
mustKnow: Carbon has 4 valence electrons — can form 4 covalent bonds.
Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons — forms 3 bonds + 1 lone pair.
Oxygen has 6 valence electrons — forms 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs.
Halogens have 7 valence electrons — form 1 bond + 3 lone pairs.

subtopics.title: VSEPR Theory and Molecular Geometry
keyPoints: VSEPR: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory.
Electron groups (bonds + lone pairs) around a central atom stay as far apart as possible.
sp³ hybridization: tetrahedral geometry, bond angle 109.5° (e.g., CH₄, NH₃, H₂O).
sp² hybridization: trigonal planar geometry, bond angle 120° (e.g., C₂H₄).
sp hybridization: linear geometry, bond angle 180° (e.g., C₂H₂).
Other hybridizations: dsp³ (trigonal bipyramidal), d²sp³ (octahedral).
mustKnow: Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs — reduces bond angles.
NH₃: trigonal pyramidal (107°), H₂O: bent (104.5°) due to lone pair repulsion.
Sigma (σ) bonds: end-on overlap, stronger. Pi (π) bonds: sideways p-orbital overlap, weaker.
examTraps: Do not confuse molecular geometry (shape) with electron group geometry.
A double bond = 1 sigma + 1 pi bond; triple bond = 1 sigma + 2 pi bonds.

summary: Industrial processes for obtaining and refining pure metals from nature: mining, ore concentration, roasting/calcination, reduction, electrolysis, and refining.

subtopics.title: Reactivity Series and Extraction Methods
keyPoints: Highly reactive metals (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al): extracted by electrolysis of molten ore/chloride.
Moderately reactive metals (Zn to Pb): extracted by carbon reduction (below carbon in series).
Low reactivity metals (Cu, Ag, Au, Pt): found as pure elements or extracted by roasting.
Carbon is included in the reactivity series as a reference for extraction methods.
The tendency to be oxidized is linked to a metal's position — lower metals resist oxidation.
mustKnow: Potassium → Aluminum: electrolysis of molten ore.
Zinc → Lead: reduction with carbon in a blast furnace.
Copper, Silver, Gold, Platinum: found pure or extracted by simple heating.
Thermite reaction: Al reduces Fe₂O₃ or CuO (Al + metal oxide → Al₂O₃ + metal + heat).
examTraps: Aluminum is high in the series — CANNOT be extracted by heating with carbon.
Calcium is extracted by electrolysis, NOT by carbon reduction.
Copper CAN be extracted using carbon (it is below carbon in the series).

subtopics.title: Ore Processing: Concentration to Refining
keyPoints: Stage 1 — Concentration: Gravity separation (heavy ore settles), Froth floatation (sulfide ores, ore wetted by pine oil), Magnetic separation (magnetic rollers), Leaching (solvent dissolves ore — for Al, Ag, Au).
Stage 1b — Thermal treatment: Roasting (sulfide ore + O₂ → metal oxide + SO₂), Calcination (carbonate ore heated → metal oxide + CO₂).
Stage 2 — Reduction: Metal oxide + reducing agent → crude metal.
Stage 3 — Refining: Electrolytic refining produces pure metal.
mustKnow: Zinc blende (ZnS) → ZnO by ROASTING.
Smithsonite (ZnCO₃) → ZnO by CALCINATION.
Coke provides both the reducing agent (C → CO) and heat.
Limestone (CaCO₃) removes acidic impurities (SiO₂) as slag (CaSiO₃).
Electrolytic refining of copper: IMPURE copper = anode, PURE copper = cathode, CuSO₄ = electrolyte.
Anode mud: insoluble impurities (Ag, Au, Pt) settle below anode.
examTraps: Electrolysis is expensive due to large electricity requirements.
Leaching is specifically used for Al, Ag, and Au.
Highly reactive metals are found as chloride ores, not as pure elements.

subtopics.title: Iron Extraction — Blast Furnace
keyPoints: Iron found as Hematite (Fe₂O₃), not pure element.
Zone 1 (bottom): C + O₂ → CO₂ (exothermic, provides heat).
Zone 2 (middle): CO₂ + C → 2CO (reducing agent produced).
Zone 3 (top): Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (reduction of iron ore).
Limestone decomposition: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂.
Slag formation: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (neutralizes acidic impurities).
Iron is tapped from bottom; slag floats on top and is removed separately.
mustKnow: Hematite = Fe₂O₃. Slag = CaSiO₃ (calcium silicate). Coke = source of C and heat.
Iron extraction is a continuous process to save reheating costs.
Hot air blown into bottom reacts with coke to produce CO₂ and heat.

subtopics.title: Aluminum Extraction — Hall-Héroult Process
keyPoints: Bauxite is purified to Al₂O₃ (alumina).
Al₂O₃ is dissolved in molten cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) to lower melting point.
Cathode: graphite lining of the steel case. Anode: graphite blocks.
At cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (reduction, aluminum ions gain electrons).
At anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ (oxidation, oxygen ions lose electrons).
Anode carbon reacts with O₂ to form CO₂, causing the anode to wear away.
mustKnow: Cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) lowers the melting point of Al₂O₃ without interfering with the reaction.
Graphite anodes must be replaced regularly because they react with oxygen to form CO₂.
The steel case is lined with graphite which acts as the cathode.

subtopics.title: Sodium Extraction — Down's Process
keyPoints: Sodium is extracted by electrolysis of molten NaCl.
Pure sodium metal forms at the cathode.
Chlorine gas is produced at the anode.
The process requires large amounts of electricity.
mustKnow: Electrolysis of molten salt (not aqueous solution) is required because Na would react with water.
This is the standard method for extracting highly reactive metals.

topic: Block 9: Aromatic Chemistry and Reaction Mechanisms
summary: This block covers aromatic electrophilic substitution reactions, the reagents and conditions for common transformations, nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2), and key organic reactions such as oxidation, ozonolysis, esterification, and condensation.

subtopics.title: Aromatic Electrophilic Substitution
keyPoints: Nitration: C₆H₆ + HNO₃/H₂SO₄ → C₆H₅NO₂ (nitrobenzene). The active species is the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺).
Halogenation: C₆H₆ + Br₂/FeBr₃ → C₆H₅Br (bromobenzene). FeBr₃ is a catalyst.
Sulfonation: C₆H₆ + SO₃/H₂SO₄ → C₆H₅SO₃H (benzenesulfonic acid).
Friedel-Crafts Alkylation: C₆H₆ + RCl/AlCl₃ → C₆H₅R (e.g., ethylbenzene from C₂H₅Cl/AlCl₃).
Friedel-Crafts Acylation: C₆H₆ + RCOCl/AlCl₃ → C₆H₅COR (e.g., acetophenone from CH₃COCl/AlCl₃).
Gattermann-Koch: C₆H₆ + CO/HCl/AlCl₃ → C₆H₅CHO (benzaldehyde).
mustKnow: Benzene to nitrobenzene: HNO₃/Conc. H₂SO₄.
Benzene to bromobenzene: Br₂/FeBr₃ (catalyst required — unlike alkenes which add Br₂ directly).
Phenol to 2,4,6-tribromophenol: Br₂ water (no catalyst needed due to -OH activation).
Toluene to 2-nitrotoluene: HNO₃/H₂SO₄ (toluene is more reactive than benzene due to CH₃ group).
Phenol to salicylic acid: CO₂/NaOH (Kolbe-Schmitt reaction).
Toluene to benzoic acid: KMnO₄ (side-chain oxidation).
Benzene to cyclohexane: H₂/Ni (hydrogenation).
Ethyne to benzene: red-hot iron tube, 873K (cyclotrimerization).
examTraps: Br₂ water reacts with phenol (no catalyst), but Br₂/FeBr₃ is needed for benzene.
Order matters for disubstitution: Cl₂/FeCl₃ THEN HNO₃/H₂SO₄ gives m-chloronitrobenzene (Cl is ortho/para directing but nitro is meta-directing).
For CH₃Cl then Cl₂/FeCl₃ on benzene: first alkylation (CH₃Cl/AlCl₃), then chlorination → p-chlorotoluene (methyl is ortho/para directing).

subtopics.title: Nucleophilic Substitution: SN1 and SN2
keyPoints: SN2: one-step concerted mechanism, backside attack, inversion of configuration, second-order kinetics.
SN2 rate: CH₃⁺ → CH₃CH₂⁺ → (CH₃)₂CH⁺ → (CH₃)₃C⁺ (faster for less hindered substrates).
SN1: two-step mechanism, carbocation intermediate, first-order kinetics, racemization.
SN1 rate: (CH₃)₃C⁺ → (CH₃)₂CH⁺ → CH₃CH₂⁺ → CH₃⁺ (faster for more stable carbocations).
Carbocation stability: tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl.
Strong nucleophiles favor SN2; weak nucleophiles and protic solvents favor SN1.
mustKnow: CH₃Br undergoes SN2 fastest (least steric hindrance).
(CH₃)₃CBr undergoes SN1 fastest (forms stable tertiary carbocation).
Lucas test distinguishes 1°, 2°, and 3° alcohols based on carbocation stability.
examTraps: SN2 has first-order kinetics? No — it is second order (rate depends on both substrate and nucleophile).
SN1 has first-order kinetics (rate depends only on substrate concentration).

subtopics.title: Oxidation, Reduction, and Key Reactions
keyPoints: Primary alcohol + K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄ (distillation) → aldehyde.
Primary alcohol + K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄ (reflux) → carboxylic acid.
Secondary alcohol + K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄ → ketone (no further oxidation).
Ketones are resistant to oxidation — they do NOT react with KMnO₄ (unlike aldehydes).
Tollens test: aldehyde + Tollens reagent → silver mirror (ketones give no reaction).
Fehling test: aldehyde → red Cu₂O precipitate (ketones give no reaction).
Iodoform test: CH₃CH(OH)R or CH₃COR + I₂/NaOH → yellow CHI₃ precipitate (e.g., ethanol, propanone).
2,4-DNP: aldehydes/ketones + 2,4-DNP → colored hydrazone precipitate.
HCN adds to carbonyls → cyanohydrin.
Ozonolysis: cyclohexene + O₃ then (CH₃)₂S → hexane-1,6-dial.
Cold alkaline KMnO₄: cyclohexene → cyclohexane-1,2-diol (syn dihydroxylation).
Esterification: RCOOH + R'OH (conc. H₂SO₄) → RCOOR' + H₂O.
Claisen condensation: two ester molecules react in base.
Aldol condensation: two aldehyde/ketone molecules react in base.
mustKnow: Propanoic acid → propanoyl chloride: SOCl₂ or PCl₅.
CH₃CH₂COCl = propanoyl chloride.
CH₃CH₂CONHCH₃ = N-methylpropanamide.
4-methylpentanal = an aldehyde with 5-carbon chain and methyl on carbon 4.
FeCl₃ test: gives violet color with phenols (not with alcohols or acids).
Positive Iodoform test: ethanol, propanone, and any methyl ketone or secondary alcohol with CH₃CH(OH)-.
examTraps: Propanone (ketone) does NOT react with KMnO₄ — this distinguishes it from aldehydes.
Tollens test distinguishes aldehydes (silver mirror) from ketones (no reaction).
The Iodoform test is positive for ethanol AND propanone — both give yellow CHI₃.
Markovnikov's rule: H adds to the carbon with more H atoms (major product of 2-methyl-2-butene + HBr is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane).
Acid strength increases with electron-withdrawing groups: CCl₃COOH > CHCl₂COOH > CH₂ClCOOH > CH₃COOH.
Methyl propanoate = CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ (not ethyl ethanoate).

topic: Block 1: Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Energy
summary: SHM is periodic motion where acceleration is proportional to negative displacement (a = -ω²x). This block covers mass-spring systems, pendulums, and energy transformations in oscillatory motion.

subtopics.title: Fundamentals of SHM
keyPoints: SHM: acceleration is directly proportional to displacement and directed toward equilibrium (a = -ω²x).
Angular frequency: ω = √(k/m).
Period (T): T = 2π/ω = 2π√(m/k) for mass-spring; T = 2π√(L/g) for simple pendulum.
Frequency (f): f = 1/T = ω/2π.
Speed is maximum at equilibrium position (x = 0).
Acceleration and potential energy are maximum at maximum displacement (amplitude, x = A).
mustKnow: Total energy E = ½kA² remains constant in the absence of friction.
KE = ½k(A² - x²), PE = ½kx².
At equilibrium: KE is max, PE = 0. At amplitude: PE is max, KE = 0.
examTraps: Do not confuse angular frequency (ω) with frequency (f) — ω = 2πf.
The period of a pendulum depends only on length and gravity, NOT on mass.

topic: Block 2: Damped, Resonant, and Coupled Oscillations
summary: Real oscillators experience damping. This block covers underdamped, critically damped, and overdamped systems, resonance, quality factor, and coupled oscillators with normal modes.

subtopics.title: Damping and Resonance
keyPoints: Damping: a force (friction/viscosity) opposing motion, usually proportional to velocity.
Underdamped (b² < 4mk): system oscillates with decreasing amplitude.
Critically damped (b² = 4mk): returns to equilibrium fastest without oscillating.
Overdamped (b² > 4mk): returns to equilibrium slowly without oscillating.
Resonance: occurs when driving frequency equals natural frequency → large amplitude.
Quality factor (Q = f₀/Δf): measures how underdamped a system is; high-Q = sharp resonance.
mustKnow: Critical damping is the optimal condition for shock absorbers and door closers.
Q-factor relates to energy stored vs energy lost per cycle.

subtopics.title: Coupled Oscillators
keyPoints: Coupled oscillators: independent oscillators that influence each other's motion.
Normal modes: specific patterns where all parts vibrate at the same frequency.
Symmetric mode: masses move in-phase; coupling spring is not stretched.
Antisymmetric mode: masses move out-of-phase; coupling spring is stretched (higher frequency).
mustKnow: Any complex motion of a coupled system can be expressed as a combination of normal modes.
The antisymmetric mode always has a higher frequency than the symmetric mode.

summary: Waves transfer energy without bulk matter transport. This block covers wave types, the wave equation, sound speed, the Doppler effect, beats, and standing waves in pipes.

subtopics.title: Wave Properties
keyPoints: Wave: disturbance that propagates energy and momentum without bulk transport of matter.
Mechanical waves require a medium (sound); non-mechanical waves do not (light).
Longitudinal: particle motion parallel to propagation (sound).
Transverse: particle motion perpendicular to propagation (light, ripples).
Speed: v = fλ.
Wave equation: ∂²y/∂t² = v² ∂²y/∂x².
mustKnow: Sound speed in air ≈ 340 m/s, depends on temperature (v ∝ √T).
Superposition principle: resultant displacement is the sum of individual wave displacements.

subtopics.title: Doppler Effect and Standing Waves
keyPoints: Doppler effect: change in frequency due to relative motion. f' = f(v ± v₀)/(v ∓ vₛ).
Beats: periodic intensity variations from two waves of slightly different frequencies (f_beat = |f₁ - f₂|).
Standing waves: superposition of two identical waves traveling in opposite directions.
Nodes: points of zero displacement.
Open-open pipe: all harmonics (n = 1, 2, 3...).
Open-closed pipe: only odd harmonics (n = 1, 3, 5...).
mustKnow: Use the correct sign convention for Doppler: +v₀ if observer moves toward source; -vₛ if source moves toward observer.
Fundamental frequency (first harmonic) is the lowest resonant frequency.

summary: Reflection obeys θᵢ = θᵣ. This block covers plane mirrors, image formation, mirror rotation, and curved mirrors (concave and convex) with the mirror formula and sign convention.

subtopics.title: Plane Mirrors
keyPoints: Law of reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection (θᵢ = θᵣ).
Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in the same plane.
Plane mirrors form virtual, erect, same-size, and laterally inverted images.
Image distance behind mirror equals object distance in front.
Rotating a mirror by θ rotates the reflected ray by 2θ.
Minimum mirror height to view full image = half the person's height.
mustKnow: For a point object 10 cm from a plane mirror, the image is 10 cm behind the mirror → distance between object and image = 20 cm.
Lateral inversion: left-right reversal of the image.

subtopics.title: Curved Mirrors
keyPoints: Concave mirror: converging mirror; can form real or virtual images depending on object position.
Convex mirror: diverging mirror; always forms virtual, upright, and diminished images.
Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v.
Magnification: M = v/u.
Sign convention (Real is Positive): f is positive for concave mirrors, negative for convex.
Applications: concave in telescopes, solar cookers, headlights; convex in rear-view mirrors.
mustKnow: Object at C (center of curvature): image is real, inverted, same size at C.
Object between F and mirror: image is virtual, upright, and magnified.
Object at F: no image is formed (rays are parallel after reflection).
R = 2f (radius of curvature = twice focal length).
examTraps: Convex mirrors have negative focal length — always use negative f in calculations.
Do not confuse concave (converging) with convex (diverging).

topic: Block 5: Geometrical Optics — Refraction and Lenses
summary: Refraction changes the direction of light when it enters a new medium. This block covers Snell's law, refractive index, apparent depth, lenses, the lensmakers formula, optical instruments, and vision correction.

subtopics.title: Refraction
keyPoints: Refraction: change in direction due to change in speed when entering a new medium obliquely.
Snell's law: n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂.
Absolute refractive index (n): n = c/v.
Light bends toward the normal when entering a denser medium (slowing down).
Apparent depth (d_app): d_app = d_real / n.
Relative refractive index < 1: light speeds up and bends away from the normal.
mustKnow: n_air ≈ 1.00, n_water ≈ 1.33, n_glass ≈ 1.50, n_diamond ≈ 2.42.
Refraction always involves a change in speed (yes) and direction (if incident obliquely).
If light enters perpendicularly, it is NOT refracted (passes straight through).

subtopics.title: Lenses and Optical Instruments
keyPoints: Convex (converging) lens: brings parallel rays to a focus; positive focal length.
Concave (diverging) lens: spreads parallel rays; negative focal length.
Lens formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f.
Lensmakers formula: 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R₁ + 1/R₂).
Refractive power: P = 1/f (unit: dioptre, D).
Simple microscope: one lens. Compound microscope: objective + eyepiece (multiple lenses).
Camera with a lens collects more light than a pinhole camera.
mustKnow: For a converging lens: object beyond 2F → real, inverted, diminished image at 2F. Object at 2F → real, inverted, same size. Object between F and 2F → real, inverted, magnified. Object within F → virtual, upright, magnified.
Diverging lens always forms virtual, upright, and diminished images.
Spherical aberration: caused by imperfect shape. Chromatic aberration: caused by different refractive indices for different wavelengths.
examTraps: Power of a diverging lens is NEGATIVE (P = -1/|f|).
Do not confuse myopia correction (concave lens) with hyperopia correction (convex lens).

subtopics.title: The Human Eye
keyPoints: Myopia (near-sightedness): eyeball too long, image forms in front of retina → corrected with concave (diverging) lenses.
Hyperopia (far-sightedness): eyeball too short, image forms behind retina → corrected with convex (converging) lenses.
mustKnow: Concave lens diverges light before it enters the eye, moving the image back onto the retina.
Convex lens converges light more strongly, moving the image forward onto the retina.

summary: Modern physics covers atomic models from Thomson to Bohr, nuclear physics (isotopes, isobars, isotones), radioactivity, X-rays, and wave-particle duality.

subtopics.title: Atomic Models
keyPoints: Mechanical Atomic Model: atom as smallest indivisible particle (explains chemical combinations like constant proportion, multiple proportion, Gay-Lussac's law).
Thomson's Plum Pudding Model: positive sphere with embedded electrons — explains electrovalent bonding but lacks detail about atomic structure.
Rutherford Model: small, dense, positive nucleus from gold foil experiment (Geiger-Marsden); atom is mostly empty space.
Rutherford's limitations: cannot explain atomic stability or line spectra (electrons should radiate and spiral in).
Bohr Model: electrons orbit in discrete energy levels; angular momentum is quantized (L = mvr = nh/2π).
Bohr's quantum condition: electron wavelength fits the circumference of orbit a whole number of times.
mustKnow: Gold foil experiment: alpha particles scattered by electrostatic repulsion from the nucleus.
Impact parameter (b) relates to kinetic energy, target atomic number (Z), and scattering angle.
Nuclear radius: R = R₀A^(1/3) where R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm.
The nucleus is much smaller than the atom.
examTraps: Rutherford expected small-angle scattering but observed large-angle deflections — this led to the nuclear model.
Bohr's model has no theoretical basis for selecting allowed orbits — it was empirically derived.

subtopics.title: Nuclear Physics
keyPoints: Nuclide: a particular type of nucleus (characterized by Z and A).
Isotopes: same Z, different N (different neutrons).
Isobars: same A (mass number), different Z. Isotones: same N, different A.
Nucleon: generic name for protons and neutrons. N = A - Z.
Alpha particle: helium nucleus (⁴₂He). Beta: fast electron. Gamma: high-energy EM wave.
Half-life (T₁/₂): time for half a radioactive sample to decay.
X-rays: produced when high-speed electrons decelerate on a metal target in a vacuum.
mustKnow: Alpha decay reduces A by 4 and Z by 2. Beta decay increases Z by 1 (A unchanged).
Neutron has slightly larger mass than proton; electron is much lighter; photon has zero rest mass.
Elementary particles: fermions (half-integer spin, obey Pauli) and bosons (integer spin, Bose-Einstein statistics).
examTraps: Hydrogen is NOT an elementary particle — it is an atom.
Protons and neutrons are NOT elementary — they are made of quarks.
Bosons do NOT obey the Pauli exclusion principle (multiple bosons can occupy the same state).

subtopics.title: Hydrogen Spectrum
keyPoints: Line spectrum: produced by gases at low pressure — each element has a unique fingerprint spectrum.
Five series: Lyman (UV), Balmer (visible), Paschen, Brackett, Pfund (IR).
Balmer series: visible region, n_f = 2. Lyman series: UV, n_f = 1.
Rydberg constant (R_H): used in empirical formula for hydrogen spectral lines.
Energy levels: E_n = -13.6/n² eV. Ground state: n = 1, E = -13.6 eV.
ΔE = hf = hc/λ when electron jumps between levels.
mustKnow: Excitation energy from n=1 to n=2: 10.2 eV. From n=1 to n=3: 12.1 eV.
Electron stays in excited state for about 10⁻⁸ s before decaying.
All spectral series converge at the short-wavelength end (series limit).
